p.src: Now the king of the Kingdom of Jisai and all his high and lesser ministers watched as Great Sage Sun and Bajie mounted cloud and mist and drifted away carrying the two lesser demons. Every one of them bowed toward heaven, saying, “The tales were no falsehood. Only today have we learned that such divine immortals and living buddhas truly exist.” When the two had vanished into the distance, the king thanked Tripitaka and Sha Monk, saying, “Being but a mortal of flesh with ordinary eyes, I knew only that your eminent disciples possessed great strength and could capture the demon thieves. How could I have known that they were exalted immortals able to ride the clouds and mist?” Tripitaka said, “This poor monk possesses not the slightest magic power. Throughout the journey I have depended greatly upon these three humble disciples.” Sha Monk said, “To tell Your Majesty the truth, my eldest brother is none other than the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, now converted to the faith. He once caused havoc in Heaven. Wielding a single gold-banded cudgel, he found no match among a hundred thousand celestial soldiers, and made even the Supreme Lord Lao fearful and the Jade Emperor tremble. My second elder brother is the duly ordained Marshal of the Heavenly Reeds, who once commanded the mighty host of eighty thousand sailors of the River of Heaven. Only I, your disciple, have no powers; I am merely the former Curtain-Raising General who received the precepts. We foolish brothers are incapable of various other things, but as for capturing demons and binding monsters, seizing thieves and arresting fugitives, subduing tigers and dragons, kicking the heavens and troubling the wells, or even churning the seas and overturning rivers, we have some small acquaintance with such arts. Riding clouds and mist, summoning rain and wind, shifting the Dipper and moving the stars, carrying mountains and driving the moon—those are merely incidental skills, scarcely worth mentioning!” On hearing this, the king treated them with tenfold greater reverence. He invited the Tang monk to the seat of honor, repeatedly addressing him as “Venerable Buddha,” and called Sha Monk and the others “Bodhisattvas.” The civil and military officials of the whole court rejoiced, while all the people of the kingdom bowed in worship—but no more of that.

p.src: Meanwhile, Great Sage Sun and Bajie rode a violent wind, carried the two lesser demons to Emerald-Wave Pool at Tumbled-Rock Mountain, and halted their cloud. He breathed a breath of immortal air upon the gold-banded cudgel and cried, “Change!” It changed into a monk’s knife. He cut the ear from the blackfish monster and the lower lip from the catfish spirit, then flung them into the water and shouted, “Hurry and report to the All-Saints Dragon King that I, Grandfather Sun, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, am here. Tell him to surrender at once the original treasure from the pagoda of Golden Light Monastery in the Kingdom of Jisai, and I will spare his entire household. But if he lets slip even half a word of refusal, I shall stir this pool dry and have every old and young member of his clan put to death.”

p.src: The two lesser demons, having been spared, endured their pain and fled for their lives, dragging their chains as they plunged into the water. The soft-shelled turtles, alligators, tortoises, freshwater turtles, prawns, crabs, and fish spirits were so startled that they all crowded around and asked, “Why are you two dragging ropes and chains?” One covered his ear, shaking his head and wagging his tail; the other covered his mouth, stamping his feet and beating his breast. Amid a noisy uproar, they went straight to the Dragon King’s palace, crying, “Your Majesty, disaster has struck!” The All-Saints Dragon King was drinking with the Nine-Headed Prince Consort. When he suddenly saw the two arrive, he set down his cup and asked what disaster had occurred. The two reported at once, “While out on patrol last night, we were captured by the Tang monk and Pilgrim Sun as they swept the pagoda, and they bound us with iron chains. This morning, after we were taken before the king, Pilgrim Sun and Zhu Bajie seized us again. They cut the ear from one of us and the lip from the other, then threw us into the water and ordered us to report that they demand the treasure from the top of the pagoda.” They then related the whole affair from beginning to end in full detail. When the old dragon heard that it was Pilgrim Sun, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, he was so terrified that his soul left his body and his wits scattered to the highest heavens. Trembling, he said to his son-in-law, “Worthy son-in-law, if it were anyone else, we might contrive a plan; but if it truly is he, this bodes no good.” The prince consort laughed and said, “Set your mind at ease, honored father-in-law. Your foolish son-in-law has practiced martial arts since childhood and has met several heroes within the Four Seas. Why should I fear him? Let me go out and fight him for three rounds. I guarantee that scoundrel will bow his head and submit, not daring even to look up at me.”

p.src: Hearing this, the prince consort gave a faint, cold laugh and said, “So you are a monk fetching scriptures, meddling without cause and taking trouble upon yourself. I steal his treasure, while you fetch the Buddha’s scriptures. What concern is it of yours, and why come fight me?” Pilgrim Sun said, “You thieving monster are utterly unreasonable. It is true that I have received no favor from the king and consumed none of his food or water, so I owe him no service. But you stole his treasure, defiled his pagoda, and for years caused the monks of Golden Light Monastery to suffer unjustly. They and I belong to the same Buddhist family and share one spirit. How could I not help them clear away this injustice?” The prince consort said, “If that is how it is, I suppose you mean to stake all upon a fight. As the saying goes, ‘Once weapons are raised, no good can come of it.’ I only fear that once I begin I shall be unable to show mercy, and in a moment may take your life and prevent you from fetching the scriptures.”

p.src: The two went back and forth for more than thirty rounds, with neither gaining the victory. Zhu Bajie stood before the mountain watching them. When he saw that their battle had reached its fiercest and most engrossing point, he raised his rake and struck at the monster from behind. The monster, however, had nine heads, each ringed with eyes, and saw the attack clearly. As Bajie came from behind, the monster at once used the butt of his spade to block the rake while holding off the iron cudgel with its blade. He held out for another five or seven rounds, but could not withstand the weapons whirling at him from front and rear. Then he rolled over, leaped into the air, and revealed his true form: a nine-headed creature. Its appearance was exceedingly vicious; the mere sight of its form was enough to terrify a man to death. p.src: Zhu Bajie was alarmed at the sight and said, “Brother, in all my life I have never seen such a vicious creature. What savage essence could have spawned such a beast?” The Pilgrim said, “It truly is a rarity—truly a rarity. Let me catch up and strike it.” Our great Sage swiftly mounted his auspicious cloud, leapt into the air, and brought his iron staff down upon the creature’s head. The monster revealed its enormous true form and flew obliquely on outspread wings. With a whoosh it wheeled around and swept toward the mountain; halfway there, another head reached out, its mouth gaping like a basin of blood. It seized Bajie’s bristles in one bite and, half dragging and half hauling him, carried him down into the waters of Green Wave Pool. On reaching the Dragon Palace, it resumed its former appearance, flung Bajie to the ground, and cried, “Where are my underlings?” From within, fish spirits of mackerel, whitefish, carp, and mandarin fish, together with shelled monsters of tortoise, soft-shelled turtle, giant turtle, and alligator, surged forward as one and answered, “Here!” The royal son-in-law said, “Tie this monk up over there, so that I may avenge the scout he killed.” The spirits shoved and clamored as they carried Bajie inside. The old Dragon King came out delighted to meet them, saying, “Worthy son-in-law, you have done well! How did you capture him?” The royal son-in-law related the whole affair from beginning to end. The old Dragon King immediately ordered a feast to be laid in celebration of the victory, but of that we shall say no more.

p.src: Now Sun the Pilgrim, seeing the fiend seize Bajie, thought fearfully, “This brute is terribly formidable. If I return to court to see Master, I fear the king will laugh at me; but if I challenge it to battle, I am alone, and besides, I am unaccustomed to fighting on the water. I had better transform myself and go inside to see what the monster means to do with that idiot. If I find an opportunity, I shall steal him out, and then we can act.” Our great Sage made a hand sign, shook himself, and once more changed into a crab. Plunging into the water, he went straight to the ornamental archway. He knew this route well from the previous occasion when he had impersonated the Bull Demon King and stolen the Golden-Eyed Beast. He crawled sideways all the way beneath the palace, where once again he saw the old Dragon King, the Nine-Headed Beast, and the entire household drinking merrily together. The Pilgrim dared not approach them. Crawling beneath the eastern gallery, he saw several shrimp and crab spirits frolicking in a noisy crowd. After listening to their talk for a while, the Pilgrim imitated their manner of speech and asked, “Has that long-snouted monk whom His Highness captured died yet?” The spirits answered, “He is not dead. Can you not hear him groaning, tied beneath the western gallery?”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim quietly crawled over to the western gallery. Sure enough, the idiot was tied to a pillar, groaning. The Pilgrim went up to him and said, “Bajie, do you recognize me?” Bajie heard the voice and knew it was the Pilgrim. “Brother,” he said, “what has happened? That brute ended up capturing me instead.” The Pilgrim looked all around and, seeing no one, used his pincers to snip through the ropes and told Bajie to run. Once his hands were free, the idiot said, “Brother, they took away my weapon. What am I to do?” The Pilgrim asked, “Do you know where they put it?” Bajie said, “That monster carried it up to the palace.” The Pilgrim said, “Go and wait for me beneath the archway.” Glad to escape with his life, Bajie quietly slipped out. The Pilgrim crawled back up to the palace to look around. Beneath the left side gleamed a brilliant light: it was Bajie’s rake shining. Using a spell of invisibility, he stole out the rake, reached the archway, and called, “Bajie, catch your weapon!” Once the idiot had his rake, he said, “Brother, you go first and let old Zhu fight his way into the palace. If I win, I shall capture their whole family; if I lose and flee out, be ready to help me from the bank of the pool.” The Pilgrim was delighted and merely warned him to be careful. Bajie said, “I am not afraid of him. I have some small skill in the water myself.” Leaving him there, the Pilgrim rose backward through the water to the surface, and of him we shall say no more for now.

p.src: The Nine-Headed Beast hid the princess safely in the inner chambers, hastily seized his crescent-bladed spade, and rushed to the front palace, shouting, “You insolent, clumsy swine! How dare you act so wickedly and terrorize my household?” Bajie cursed him, saying, “You thieving monster! How dare you capture me? This battle is none of my doing—you invited me here to smash your home yourself. Hurry and return the treasure to me, so that I may report back to the king and end the matter; otherwise, I shall spare not one life in your family.” The monster had no thought of showing mercy. Gritting his teeth, he engaged Bajie in combat. The old Dragon King had now recovered his wits. Leading his dragon sons and grandsons, each armed with spear or sword, he joined the attack. Seeing that matters had turned against him, Bajie made a feint with his rake, wheeled around, and fled. The old Dragon King led the host in pursuit. In a moment they burst from the water and were all surging and churning over the surface of the pool.

The Pilgrim said, “What does it matter if it is late? Take advantage of this opportunity and go down to attack them again.
We must recover the treasure before we can return to court.”
The idiot had lost heart and enthusiasm and kept making halfhearted excuses.
The Pilgrim pressed him, saying, “Brother, do not hesitate. Lure them out as you did just now, and I shall strike them.”

p.src: As the two were discussing the matter, they heard a wild wind rolling in and saw a dismal mist gathering darkly, sweeping suddenly from the east straight toward the south. The Pilgrim looked carefully and saw that it was Erlang, the Illustrious Sage, leading the Six Brothers of Mount Mei. They had hawks and hounds with them, foxes and hares slung from poles, and musk deer and deer borne aloft. Each man wore a curved bow at his waist and held a sharp blade in his hand as they came bounding through the wind and mist. The Pilgrim said, “Bajie, those are my seven sage brothers. We should ask them to stay and help us in battle. If we succeed, this will prove a splendid opportunity indeed.” Bajie said, “If they are your brothers, we certainly ought to invite them to stay.” The Pilgrim said, “But among them is my elder brother, the Illustrious Sage, and I was once subdued by him, so I am embarrassed to face him. Go and bar their cloud-path, and call out, ‘True Lord, please halt a moment. The Great Sage Equaling Heaven is here to pay his respects.’ Once he hears that it is I, he will certainly stop. After he has alighted, I shall be able to meet him properly.”

p.src: The fool hurriedly spurred his cloud upward, blocked the party on the mountain, and shouted sternly, “True Lord, halt your procession a moment! The Great Sage Equal to Heaven asks to see you.” When the lord heard this, he immediately gave the order to halt, stopped with his six brothers, and, after exchanging greetings with Bajie, asked, “Where is the Great Sage Equal to Heaven?” Bajie replied, “He is waiting below the mountain to be summoned.” Erlang said, “Brothers, go quickly and invite him here.” The six brothers were Kang, Zhang, Yao, Li, Guo, and Zhi. Each came out of the camp and called, “Brother Sun Wukong, our elder brother invites you.” The Pilgrim stepped forward, bowed to them all, and went up the mountain with them. Lord Erlang came forward to meet him, took his hand, and supported him as they exchanged greetings. He said, “Great Sage, you escaped your great tribulation, accepted the Buddhist precepts, and became a monk. The day when your merit is complete and you ascend the lotus throne is near. Congratulations indeed!” The Pilgrim said, “I am unworthy of such praise. In the past I received immeasurable kindness from you, yet have never found the slightest chance to repay it. Though I escaped disaster and journeyed west, I still do not know what will come of my merit and practice. Now, while passing through the Kingdom of Jisai, I undertook to rescue its monks from calamity, and have come here to capture a demon and recover a treasure. By chance I saw your procession, elder brother, and boldly asked you to remain and lend me your aid. May I ask where you have come from, elder brother, and whether you would be willing to favor me?” Erlang laughed and said, “Having nothing to occupy me, I went hunting with my brothers, and we are now on our way back. I am fortunate that the Great Sage has not disdained to detain us for this meeting; it shows the affection of an old friend, and I am deeply grateful. If you ask me to join forces with you and subdue the demon, how could I disobey? But what manner of monstrous brigand dwells here?” The Six Sages said, “Have you forgotten, elder brother? This is Tumbledown Mountain, and below it lies the Dragon Palace of the Myriad Sage in the Emerald Wave Pool.” Erlang said in surprise, “The old Dragon King Myriad Sage never used to cause trouble. How did he dare steal the pagoda’s treasure?” The Pilgrim said, “Recently he took a son-in-law, a nine-headed creature that had become a demon. Father-in-law and son-in-law turned thieves together. They sent a rain of blood upon the Kingdom of Jisai and stole the Buddha’s relic treasure from the top of the Golden Ray Monastery pagoda. The king did not understand what had happened and cruelly seized and tortured the monks. Out of compassion, my master swept the pagoda last night, and there I caught two lesser demons whom they had sent to reconnoiter. This morning we escorted them to court, where they made a full confession. The king then asked my master to subdue them, and my master ordered us to come here. In our first battle, the nine-headed creature thrust a head from its waist, seized Bajie in its beak, and carried him away. I then transformed myself, went underwater, and freed Bajie. We fought another great battle only moments ago. I killed the old dragon, and those villains have withdrawn to gather the corpse and put on mourning. The two of us were just discussing how to challenge them again when we saw your stately procession arrive, elder brother. That is why we presumed to disturb you.” Erlang said, “Since the old dragon has been killed, this is precisely the time to attack before they can react. Why not wipe out their entire lair as well?” Bajie said, “That may be so, but what are we to do about the late hour?” Erlang said, “As the military maxim goes, ‘An expedition does not wait upon the hour.’ Why fear the coming of night?”

p.src: Kang, Yao, Guo, and Zhi said, “Do not be hasty, elder brother. That villain’s family is here, so he surely has nowhere to go. Second Brother Sun is an honored guest, and Zhu Ganglie too has returned to the true path. We have wine and dishes with us in camp. Let the lads kindle a fire and spread a feast here: first, to congratulate these two, and second, to renew our friendship. Let us enjoy one night together. What harm can there be in challenging them at dawn?” Erlang was delighted and said, “Worthy brothers, what you say is entirely right.” He then ordered his junior officers to make preparations. The Pilgrim said, “I would not presume to refuse your generous hospitality. But since becoming monks we all observe abstinence, and I fear there may be difficulty over meat and vegetarian fare.” Erlang said, “We have vegetarian fruits, and the wine too is suitable for abstainers.” Beneath the light of stars and moon, the brothers made the sky their canopy and the earth their mat, raising cups as they reminisced about old times.

p.src: Indeed, lonely watches are long, but nights of merriment are short. Before they knew it, the eastern sky had turned pale. After several cups of wine, Bajie was in exuberant spirits and said, “Dawn is coming. Let old Zhu go underwater and challenge them.” Erlang said, “Take care, Marshal. You need only lure him out so that my brothers and I can strike.” Bajie laughed. “I understand, I understand.” Watch him tuck up his robe, secure his rake, perform the water-dividing spell, and leap down, heading straight for the ceremonial archway. With a great shout, he fought his way into the palace hall. At that moment the dragon prince, dressed in hempen mourning clothes, was weeping over the dragon’s corpse; the dragon grandson and the royal son-in-law were in the rear preparing the coffin. Bajie charged forward cursing. He raised his rake and brought its head down with crushing force, striking the dragon prince squarely on the skull and boring nine holes through his head with a single blow. The dragon matriarch and the others were so terrified that they fled wildly inside, crying, “That long-snouted monk has killed my son too!”

p.src: When the royal son-in-law heard this, he immediately took up his crescent-bladed spade and charged out with the dragon grandson. Bajie raised his rake to meet them, fighting as he retreated until he leaped out of the water. On the bank, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven and the seven brothers surged forward together. Amid a flurry of thrusting spears and slashing blades, they chopped the dragon grandson into several slabs of flesh. Seeing that matters had gone badly, the royal son-in-law rolled over before the mountain and resumed his true form. Spreading his wings, he wheeled and soared through the air. Erlang at once took up his golden bow, fitted a silver pellet, drew the bow to its full extent, and shot upward. The monster abruptly folded its wings and skimmed close, intending to bite Erlang. Just as another head emerged halfway from its waist, Erlang’s fine hound sprang up and, with a single snapping bite, tore the head off in a welter of blood. Maddened by the pain, the monster fled for its life, heading straight for the Northern Sea. Bajie was about to pursue it, but the Pilgrim stopped him, saying, “Do not chase him. As the saying goes, ‘Do not pursue a desperate foe.’ The hound has bitten off one of his heads, so he is far more likely to die than live. Let me assume his appearance. You part the waters and chase me inside; I will seek out the princess and trick her into giving me the treasures.” Erlang and the Six Sages said, “It may be well enough not to pursue him, but leaving such a breed alive in the world will surely bring harm to later generations.” Even today there is a blood-dripping nine-headed creature, a descendant of that surviving breed.

p.src: Bajie did as instructed and parted a path through the water. The Pilgrim assumed the monster’s form and went ahead, while Bajie pursued behind him with loud shouts. As the chase drew near the Dragon Palace, the Princess Myriad Sage appeared and said, “Husband, why are you in such a panic?” The Pilgrim replied, “Bajie has won the battle and chased me in here. I fear I cannot withstand him. Quickly hide the treasures somewhere safe.” In her haste, the princess could not distinguish true from false. She went into the rear hall, brought out a box of solid gold, handed it to the Pilgrim, and said, “This is the Buddha’s treasure.” She then brought out a white jade box, handed that to the Pilgrim as well, and said, “This is the nine-leaf numinous fungus. Take these treasures and hide them. I will fight Zhu Bajie for two or three rounds and hold him off. Once you have secured the treasures, come out again and join me in battle against him.” The Pilgrim tucked the two boxes against his body, wiped a hand across his face, resumed his own appearance, and said, “Princess, look closely. Am I truly your husband?” The princess panicked and tried to snatch back the boxes. But Bajie rushed forward and struck her across the back with his rake, knocking her to the ground.

p.src: There was still the old dragon matriarch, who turned to flee. Bajie caught hold of her and had just raised his rake to strike when the Pilgrim said, “Hold! Do not kill her. Leave one alive so that we may take her back to the kingdom as proof of our achievement.” They then hauled the dragon matriarch up out of the water.

p.src: Wukong followed them ashore, bearing the two caskets. He said to Erlang, “Thanks to your mighty power, elder brother, we have recovered the treasures and swept away the fiends.” Erlang replied, “First, the king’s blessings are as boundless as Heaven; second, you worthy brothers possess immeasurable divine powers. What merit can I claim?” His brothers all said, “Since Brother Sun has accomplished his task, we shall take our leave here.” Wukong thanked them profusely and wished to keep them there so that they might meet the king together. But they would not stay, and so they led their company back to Guanjiangkou.

p.src: Wukong carried the caskets while Bajie dragged the dragon matriarch, and, half riding cloud and half riding mist, they reached the capital in moments. The monks of the Golden Light Monastery who had been released were all waiting outside the city to welcome them. When they suddenly saw the pair descend from the clouds and mist, they hurried forward, kowtowed in homage, and escorted them into the city. The king and the Tang Monk were then conversing in the great hall. One monk who had gone ahead plucked up his courage, entered the court gate, and reported, “Your Majesty, Lords Sun and Zhu have returned after capturing the thieves and recovering the treasures.” On hearing this, the king hastened down from the hall and went with the Tang Monk and Sha Monk to meet them. He thanked them endlessly for their divine achievement and at once ordered a banquet prepared in gratitude. Tripitaka said, “There is no need to bestow wine upon us yet. Let my disciples first restore the treasures to the pagoda; only then should we feast.” Tripitaka then asked Wukong, “You left the kingdom yesterday. Why have you only now returned?” Wukong gave a detailed account of how they had fought the prince consort, attacked the Dragon King, encountered the True Lord, defeated the fiends, and used transformations to trick them out of the treasures. Tripitaka, the king, and all the civil and military officials were overjoyed.

p.src: The king then asked, “Can the dragon matriarch speak human speech?” Bajie replied, “She is the Dragon King’s wife and has borne many dragon sons and grandsons. How could she not know human speech?” The king said, “Since you know human speech, quickly tell us the whole story of your thievery.” The dragon matriarch said, “I knew nothing at all about the theft of the Buddha’s treasure. It was all done by my husband, that dragon fiend, and our son-in-law, the Nine-Headed Insect. They knew that the light from your pagoda came from a Buddhist śarīra, and three years ago, when they sent down a rain of blood, they seized the opportunity to steal it.” The king asked again, “And how was the numinous fungus stolen?” The dragon matriarch replied, “My youngest daughter, Princess Wansheng, secretly entered the Great Cinnabar Heaven and stole the Queen Mother’s nine-leaf numinous fungus from before the Hall of Numinous Heaven. Nourished by the immortal essence of this fungus, the śarīra will remain incorrupt for a thousand years and shine for ten thousand. If it is used to sweep underground or across a field, ten thousand rays of rosy light and a thousand streams of auspicious vapor will immediately appear. Now that you have taken it back, my husband is dead, my sons are wiped out, my son-in-law is slain, and my daughter has perished. I beg you, spare my life!” Bajie said, “We certainly will not spare you.” Wukong said, “Not every member of a family is guilty. I will spare you, but you must guard the pagoda for me forever.” The dragon matriarch said, “A wretched life is better than a good death. So long as you spare my life, I will do whatever you command.” Wukong called for an iron chain. An attendant officer immediately brought an iron chain and ran it through the dragon matriarch’s shoulder blades. He told Sha Monk, “Invite the king to come and watch us restore the pagoda.”

p.src: The king immediately ordered his procession prepared. Taking Tripitaka by the hand, he left the court with the many civil and military officials and proceeded to the Golden Light Monastery. Wukong climbed the pagoda, placed the śarīra inside the treasure vase at the summit of its thirteenth story, and chained the dragon matriarch to the central pillar. He recited a spell and summoned the local Earth God, the City God, and the monastery’s guardian deities. He ordered them to bring the dragon matriarch one meal every three days to keep her alive; should there be the slightest failure, they would be executed at once. The gods silently accepted the command. Wukong then used the numinous fungus to sweep every story of the thirteen-story pagoda, after which he placed it in the vase to nourish the śarīra. Thus the old was restored as new: ten thousand rays of rosy light and a thousand streams of auspicious vapor appeared, once more visible in every direction and admired by all four neighboring kingdoms. After they came down through the pagoda gate, the king thanked them, saying, “Had the venerable Buddha and the three Bodhisattvas not come here, how could this affair ever have been brought to light?”

p.src: Wukong said, “Your Majesty, the name ‘Golden Light’ is inauspicious and suggests nothing enduring: gold is a thing that passes from hand to hand, while light is an aura that flickers. Since this poor monk has taken such pains on your behalf, rename this monastery the Dragon-Subduing Monastery, so that your realm may endure forever.” The king immediately ordered the name changed and a new plaque hung, inscribed: “Imperially Commissioned Dragon-Subduing Monastery for the Protection of the Realm.” On one side, the imperial banquet was being prepared; on the other, painters were summoned to make portraits of the master and his three disciples, whose names were inscribed upon the Five-Phoenix Tower. The king arrayed his imperial procession to see the Tang Monk and his disciples on their way and bestowed gold and jade upon them in recompense.
